newsitem.title: GERMANY: Congressmen want recognition of German spy-swapper.
newsitem.headline: Congressmen want recognition of German spy-swapper.

text.p: Two senior members of the U.S. Congress on Wednesday urged Bonn to recognise the achievements of a controversial lawyer in communist East Germany who organised Cold War spy swaps.

The congressmen said the services of Wolfgang Vogel -- whose superpower exchanges date back to the 1962 handover of U.S. pilot Gary Powers for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel -- had gone unrecognised for too long.

"The German government should arrange to recognise what he has done in the past," Benjamin Gilman, the Republican chairman of the House of Representatives' International Relations Committee, told a news briefing in Bonn.

A German court convicted Vogel last year of extorting money from East Germans who enlisted him to help them emigrate, and who usually had to leave behind most of their property and money. Vogel received a fine and a two-year suspended jail term but both he and state prosecutors have appealed.
Another court acquitted him later last year of similar allegations involving different emigrants.
The urbane Vogel provokes mixed reactions in united Germany.
Some regard him as a hero who helped nearly 34,000 political prisoners and 215,000 East Germans to freedom in the West, albeit in return for hefty hard currency payments from Bonn to East Berlin.
Others brand the man who liked to drive around east Germany in a gold-coloured Mercedes as an opportunist who used his connections on both sides of the Berlin Wall for personal gain.

"We think he has done a great deal of good over the years and this needs to be taken into account in his present situation." said Tom Lantos, a Democrat member of the committee delegation visiting Bonn.

The congressmen said they had not raised Vogel's case during talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Tuesday but added they would discuss the matter with other political leaders during their stay in Germany.
Gilman and Lantos, who met Vogel on Wednesday, did not say what sort of recognition they thought he should receive.
